raw:
These ten hypotheses come from three analogies: epistasis, where strong backgrounds benefit less from a good mutation, diminishing returns, and redundancy of parallel paths. I added conv-after-conv synergy as a contrast to the saturation cases. They come from reasoning alone, with no benchmark data or searches run, so none is checked against the three datasets.

1. Edge 4 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 is skip_connect. The identity shortcut already gives node 3 a strong parallel path, so the extra conv is redundant.
2. Edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3. Two strong parallel routes into node 3 saturate.
3. Edge 1 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 is skip_connect. This is the early-edge counterpart of hypothesis 1 and tests whether redundancy holds for early edges too.
4. Edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 1 is nor_conv_3x3. This is the 0→2→3 chain, where stacked convs build depth and receptive field, so the effect is synergy rather than saturation.
5. Edge 4 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 0 is nor_conv_3x3. The same synergy applies on the 0→1→3 chain.
6. Edge 4 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 0 is none. Node 1 then receives no input, so edge 4 carries nothing. A mechanistic reader would expect this, so it serves as a sanity anchor.
7. Edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 5 currently holds none than when it holds anything else. Filling an empty path gains more than upgrading an existing op, which is the diminishing-returns pattern.
8. Edge 3 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 currently holds skip_connect. Replacing identity with conv gains less than replacing none or pool, because skip already supplies most of the benefit.
9. Edge 3 to skip_connect helps less when edge 5 is nor_conv_3x3. A strong alternative route makes the shortcut's marginal gradient-flow benefit smaller.
10. Edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 5 currently holds skip_connect than when it holds avg_pool_3x3. Pool is the weaker op to replace, so the swap gains more. The skip case is the main test of whether the replaced-op ordering is stable across datasets.
